newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe ostrich industry seen with bright future.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe ostrich industry seen with bright future.

text.p: Zimbabwe's ostrich industry is on track for further growth despite earlier fears that its major European market might be threatened, an industry official said on Wednesday.
Recent reports said Zimbabwe might gradually lose its market in Europe where some countries were now breeding their own birds from the livestock imported from the southern African country.

"We don't believe that Europe is going to have an impact on our market. Their climate and the high cost of land and labour is against them. The situation there is not conducive to large-scale ostrich production," said Mark Rogers, vice chairman of The Ostrich Producers Association of Zimbabwe (TOPAZ).
"The people to worry about are the Chinese, who are developing a strong ostrich industry," he added.
But Rogers acknowledged that there was now a shift towards exporting slaughtered birds and skin instead of live ostriches.

"The live export market is slowly dying down. Eventually the only (live) exports that will take place will be for pedigree (superior) birds," Rogers told Reuters, adding Zimbabwe was operating two abattoirs approved by the European Union (EU).

He said most of the meat was Europe-bound, mainly to Belgium and Switzerland, with the top-grade cuts fetching about $10 per kilogram, while a steady market for ostrich skin was growing in the USA and Japan.
TOPAZ's trading company, Copro Limited, says it has since mid-1996 exported some 100 tonnes of premium quality ostrich meat to Europe, after gaining export approval from the EU.
Copro managing director Chris Bradshaw said the company expected to export 300 tonnes during 1997, netting around $3.5 million and a further $5.25 million from the sale of ostrich skin.
Rogers said the ostrich industry had grown tremendously since he set up the first farm in Zimbabwe in 1985, possibly the first of its kind in the world outside South Africa.
There are about 180 ostrich farmers in the country, he said, adding there was now a drive towards expanding the industry to include small-scale producers.

While ostrich production was proving economically viable, most small-scale farmers lacked the necessary financial resources to venture into the industry, with banks reluctant to give loans to applicants without collateral support, he said.
TOPAZ, Rogers added, was now considering seeking an international donor to guarantee loans from commercial banks.
